claim: Transcription occurs in stochastic bursts.
source: Transcription occurs in stochastic bursts.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the following sentence.

claim: Early models based upon RNA hybridisation studies suggest bursting dynamics arise from alternating inactive and permissive states.
source: Early models based upon RNA hybridisation studies suggest bursting dynamics arise from alternating inactive and permissive states.
evidence: This claim references early models and is supported by the literature context.

claim: The data indicate a continuum of transcriptional states, with a slowly fluctuating initiation rate converting the gene between different levels of activity, interspersed with extended periods of inactivity.
source: In contrast to early models, our data indicate a continuum of transcriptional states, with a slowly fluctuating initiation rate converting the gene between different levels of activity, interspersed with extended periods of inactivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the experimental data and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The upper limit of the lifetime of fluctuations in elongation rate is 40 s.
source: We place an upper limit of 40 s on the lifetime of fluctuations in elongation rate, with initiation rate variations persisting an order of magnitude longer.
evidence: This is derived from FRAP simulations and experimental comparisons shown in Figure 4.

claim: Initiation rate variations persist an order of magnitude longer than elongation rate fluctuations.
source: We place an upper limit of 40 s on the lifetime of fluctuations in elongation rate, with initiation rate variations persisting an order of magnitude longer.
evidence: This is supported by autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: TATA mutations reduce the accessibility of high activity states.
source: TATA mutations reduce the accessibility of high activity states, leaving the lifetime of on- and off-states unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on TATA mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: TATA mutations leave the lifetime of on- and off-states unchanged.
source: TATA mutations reduce the accessibility of high activity states, leaving the lifetime of on- and off-states unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of switching rates in Figure 5E.

claim: A continuum or spectrum of gene states potentially enables a wide dynamic range for cell responses to stimuli.
source: A continuum or spectrum of gene states potentially enables a wide dynamic range for cell responses to stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Bursting transcription is conserved in all forms of life, from prokaryotes to mammalian cells and tissues.
source: Bursting transcription is conserved in all forms of life, from prokaryotes (Chong et al., 2014) to mammalian cells and tissues (Suter et al., 2011; Bahar Halpern et al., 2015; Harper et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The irregular nature of transcriptional bursting is proposed to be a major driver of spontaneous heterogeneity in gene expression.
source: The irregular nature of transcriptional bursting is proposed to be a major driver of spontaneous heterogeneity in gene expression, which in turn drives diversity of cell behaviour in differentiation and disease (Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Eldar and Elowitz, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bursting reflects the underlying mechanisms of transcriptional regulation.
source: Bursting reflects the underlying mechanisms of transcriptional regulation, and measures of bursting can reveal the dynamic processes absent from standard population average measures of RNA expression.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the one state model, transcription occurs with a constant probability.
source: In the one state model, transcription occurs with a constant probability, which for moderately and strongly transcribed genes, will generate a low variance in their total transcribed RNA per cell.
evidence: This describes a theoretical model.

claim: In budding yeast, the variance in RNA abundance measured by smFISH can fit the one state scenario, where the distribution of RNA per cell is well characterised by a Poisson distribution.
source: In some contexts, notably budding yeast (Zenklusen et al., 2008), the variance in RNA abundance measured by single molecule RNA fluorescence in situ hybridisation (smFISH) (Femino et al., 1998; Mueller et al., 2013) can fit this one state scenario, where the distribution of RNA per cell is well characterised by a Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the random telegraph (two state) model, the gene switches stochastically between an active state and an inactive state.
source: In this model, the gene switches stochastically between an active state, where mRNA production occurs with constant probability per unit time, and an inactive state, with no mRNA production.
evidence: This describes a theoretical model.

claim: The two-state model can predict the observed extra spread in transcript abundance in the cell population.
source: The extra state increases the potential variability in output from cells, and can therefore predict the observed extra spread in transcript abundance in the cell population (Singer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Burst size and frequency are quantities that can be modulated by extracellular signals.
source: A rethink is required, not least because of recent work demonstrating burst size and frequency are quantities that can be modulated by extracellular signals (Molina et al., 2013; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014; Senecal et al., 2014) and cell properties such as volume and cell cycle stage (Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015; Muramoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Burst size and frequency can be modulated by cell properties such as volume and cell cycle stage.
source: A rethink is required, not least because of recent work demonstrating burst size and frequency are quantities that can be modulated by extracellular signals (Molina et al., 2013; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014; Senecal et al., 2014) and cell properties such as volume and cell cycle stage (Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015; Muramoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An array of MS2 stem loops is inserted after the promoter of a gene of interest to visualize transcription in living cells.
source: An array of sequence encoding stem loops, such as MS2 or PP7, is inserted after the promoter of a gene of interest. When the gene is transcribed, the nascent RNA stem loops are detected with a fluorescent MS2 (MCP) or PP7 (PCP) coat protein, which is constitutively co-expressed.
evidence: This describes the MS2 system methodology.

claim: The intensity of the transcription spot reflects the instantaneous nascent RNA load at the gene.
source: The intensity of the spot reflects the instantaneous nascent RNA load at the gene and changes in spot intensity reflect how the RNA load fluctuates over time.
evidence: This is a description of how the MS2 system works.

claim: The exponential nature of the 'ON' and 'OFF' time durations of the transcript spot was related to the two state model.
source: Previous work has interpreted the appearance and disappearance of transcription spots in terms of 'bursty' transcription (Muramoto et al., 2010; Masaki et al., 2013). Here, the exponential nature of the 'ON' and 'OFF' time durations of the transcript spot was related to the two state model, with the exponential behaviour proposed to reflect rate-limiting steps in transitions between the active and inactive states.
evidence: This describes prior interpretations in the literature.

claim: An MS2 array was integrated after the promoter of the endogenous actin5 locus in Dictyostelium cells.
source: To monitor transcriptional dynamics in living cells, we integrated an array of MS2 stem loops after the promoter of the endogenous actin5 locus, a strongly expressed actin gene in undifferentiated Dictyostelium cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental system used in the study.

claim: Actin5 is a strongly expressed actin gene in undifferentiated Dictyostelium cells.
source: To monitor transcriptional dynamics in living cells, we integrated an array of MS2 stem loops after the promoter of the endogenous actin5 locus, a strongly expressed actin gene in undifferentiated Dictyostelium cells.
evidence: This is a characterization of the gene studied.

claim: The durations for which a spot is present or absent for act5 have approximately exponential distributions.
source: For most genes studied, the durations for which a spot is present or absent are often measured to have approximately exponential distributions, which is the case for act5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Muramoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exponential timescales have been inferred to represent modulation of gene activity, between the ON and OFF states of the two-state model.
source: Exponential timescales have been inferred to represent modulation of gene activity, between the ON and OFF states of the two-state model, with a rate-limiting step determining switching between states (Golding and Cox, 2006).
evidence: This describes prior interpretations in the literature.

claim: Stochastic fluctuations of a gene with no OFF state (the one state model) could give rise to pulses and intervals between pulses with exponentially distributed lifetimes.
source: A more simple possibility is that stochastic fluctuations of a gene with no OFF state - the one state model - could give rise to pulses and intervals between pulses with the experimentally observed lifetimes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the authors through simulation.

claim: A one-state model with constant polymerase initiation rates can produce exponential distributions of pulse durations.
source: The pulse duration distribution had exponential distributions at long timescales, with deviations at very short timescales (Figure 1E). This was surprising, as the exponential distribution was previously inferred to support the two-state model. Here, our simulations clearly show such a distribution can arise from a more simple one-state scenario.
evidence: This is supported by Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The average pulse duration depends strongly on the initiation rate.
source: The average pulse duration depends strongly on the initiation rate, but was also substantially sensitive to the detection threshold and frame interval specified in the simulations.
evidence: This is derived from simulations.

claim: The pulse duration is substantially sensitive to the detection threshold and frame interval.
source: The average pulse duration depends strongly on the initiation rate, but was also substantially sensitive to the detection threshold and frame interval specified in the simulations.
evidence: This is derived from simulations.

claim: The theory successfully predicts the characteristic exponential timescale of pulse duration in terms of the one state model.
source: The theory successfully predicts the characteristic exponential timescale of pulse duration in terms of the one state model, incorporating the polymerase elongation rate, the frame interval and threshold of spot detection.
evidence: This is supported by the theoretical framework and simulations shown in Figure 1G.

claim: High initiation rates are likely to give rise to large numbers of initiations per frame, giving long pulses.
source: In simple terms, the pulse duration reflects the balance between polymerase initiation and elongation or termination - in order for a spot to remain present in the next frame, a sufficient number of new polymerases must be initiated to replace the loss of spot intensity from cleaved RNA leaving the transcription site. Intuitively, high initiation rates are likely to give rise to large numbers of initiations per frame, giving long pulses.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the model.

claim: Increasing the threshold of spot detection decreases the likelihood of sufficient initiations and thus decreases the pulse duration.
source: Increasing the threshold of spot detection decreases the likelihood of sufficient initiations and thus decreases the pulse duration.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical model.

claim: The initiation and elongation rates have approximately inverse effects on spot intensity.
source: The initiation and elongation rates have approximately inverse effects, with initiation scaling directly with spot intensity (as expected intuitively) and elongation scaling inversely.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical model and simulations.

claim: Slow elongation increases spot intensity due to a polymerase 'traffic jam'.
source: The effect of slow elongation increasing spot intensity can be thought of in terms of a polymerase 'traffic jam', with several polymerases building up behind a slower one, causing a build up of nascent RNA on the gene (Darzacq et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The frame interval of observation influences the effective pulse duration.
source: Additionally, the frame interval of observation influences the effective pulse duration, as longer frame intervals increase the likelihood of a gap between pulses being missed between frames.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical model.

claim: The length of time for which a spot is visible is not simply related to switches between proposed gene states in two state models.
source: Overall, this theory shows that the length of time for which a spot is visible is not simply related to switches between proposed gene states in two state models and explains the dependence of the pulse duration on the imaging signal-to-noise (Muramoto et al., 2010) and frame interval (Masaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The autocorrelation measures the ratio of intensity fluctuations relative to the mean intensity.
source: One strategy that can be used is an autocorrelation analysis, which measures the magnitude and timescale of intensity fluctuations (Larson et al., 2011). The autocorrelation measures the ratio of intensity fluctuations relative to the mean intensity.
evidence: This describes the autocorrelation method.

claim: For a Poisson (one state) gene, the ratio of intensity fluctuations to mean intensity is related to the average number of bound polymerases.
source: For a Poisson (one state) gene, where initiations behave independently of the previous or subsequent polymerase, this ratio is related to the average number of bound polymerases, allowing the initiation rate to be estimated.
evidence: This describes a property of the Poisson model.

claim: Autocorrelation analysis of act5 transcription reveals an additional long-timescale decay of several minutes to tens of minutes.
source: Applying a similar analysis to transcription of the Dictyostelium act5 gene (Figure 2B), we find that inference of polymerase properties is complicated by an additional long-timescale decay of several minutes to tens of minutes (black dotted line).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The additional slow decay in autocorrelation indicates a model with two or more transcription states would better describe act5 transcription.
source: The additional slow decay means the RNA level at the gene is correlated beyond the dwell time at the gene of a single RNA. This argues against a Poisson model and indicates a model with two or more transcription states would better describe act5 transcription.
evidence: This is an inference from the autocorrelation data.

claim: The active periods where a spot is present are not defined by a single constant initiation rate; there are multiple 'ON' states.
source: If the autocorrelation is recalculated using only frames where a spot is present, the slow decay remains, suggesting that the active periods where a spot is present are not defined by a single constant initiation rate; in other words there are multiple 'ON' states.
evidence: This is an inference from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The RNA dwell time for act5 is approximately 190 ± 20 s.
source: By subtracting a linear estimate of the long timescale decay from the autocorrelation, we calculated estimates of the RNA dwell time and polymerase load on the gene (Larson et al., 2011). The point where the autocorrelation deviates from the long decay gives an approximation of the dwell time as 190 ± 20 s.
evidence: This is derived from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The average number of polymerases contributing to the intensity is estimated as 20–27 polymerases across 2 alleles.
source: The average number of polymerases contributing to the intensity is estimated from the magnitude of the deviation at zero lag time as 20–27 polymerases. The cells are predominantly in G2 (Muramoto and Chubb, 2008), so these autocorrelation-based estimates are for the polymerase load across 2 alleles of the act5 gene comprising the transcription spot.
evidence: This is derived from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The dwell time for the 5' MS2 insertion is around 170 s.
source: Using the difference in dwell times and assuming a constant rate of elongation across the gene, we calculate the elongation rate as 22 nt.s-1 and termination time as 60-70 s. This gives a total dwell time of around 170 s, for the 5' MS2 insertion, roughly in agreement with the autocorrelation-derived approximation on the same allele.
evidence: This is derived from FRAP measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The elongation rate for act5 is 22 nt.s-1.
source: Using the difference in dwell times and assuming a constant rate of elongation across the gene, we calculate the elongation rate as 22 nt.s-1 and termination time as 60-70 s.
evidence: This is derived from FRAP measurements.

claim: The termination time for act5 is 60-70 s.
source: Using the difference in dwell times and assuming a constant rate of elongation across the gene, we calculate the elongation rate as 22 nt.s-1 and termination time as 60-70 s.
evidence: This is derived from FRAP measurements.

claim: No significant differences in recovery time are observed for different intensity groups in FRAP experiments.
source: Figure 2D shows that no significant differences in recovery time are observed for the different intensity groups, suggesting dwell time variations are not the primary source of the spot intensity variability.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Dwell time variations are not the primary source of the spot intensity variability.
source: Figure 2D shows that no significant differences in recovery time are observed for the different intensity groups, suggesting dwell time variations are not the primary source of the spot intensity variability.
evidence: This is an inference from FRAP data.

claim: The experimental data does not lie on a single contour of constant initiation rate for a one-state gene.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that the experimental data does not lie on a single contour of constant initiation rate, consistent with the autocorrelation results in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A simple two-state implementation cannot match the variation of pulse duration and spot frequency as the detection threshold is varied.
source: Similarly, contours calculated from a simple two-state implementation, with on- and off-rates chosen to produce the experimentally observed spot frequency (details in the appendix), cannot match the variation of pulse duration and spot frequency as the detection threshold is varied (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The behaviour at high thresholds suggests a short-lived higher initiation rate.
source: Instead, the behaviour at high thresholds suggests a short-lived higher initiation rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: Dictyostelium cells are almost exclusively in G2, owing to a very short S phase and complete absence of G1.
source: Dictyostelium cells are almost exclusively in G2, owing to a very short S phase and complete absence of G1 (Muramoto and Chubb, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Almost all cells will have replicated the MS2-tagged gene and have two genes contributing to a single resolved spot.
source: Therefore almost all cells will have replicated the MS2-tagged gene and have two genes, held together by sister chromatid cohesion, contributing to a single resolved spot.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell cycle properties of Dictyostelium.

claim: Act5 transcription is not robustly detected in the first 15 min after mitosis.
source: Transcription of the unreplicated gene will not confuse analysis, as act5 transcription is not robustly detected in the first 15 min after mitosis (Muramoto et al., 2010), when euchromatin is replicated (Muramoto and Chubb, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A higher initiation rate state is possible when both copies are simultaneously active.
source: A higher initiation rate state is possible in the situation where both copies are simultaneously active - giving a potential third state with double the initiation rate of a single copy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the presence of two alleles.

claim: A two-state model of transcriptional activity does not describe the live data adequately.
source: Since a two-state model of transcriptional activity, with an 'off' state and an 'on' state of constant initiation rate, does not describe the live data adequately, we asked whether an improvement could be made by including additional active states with different initiation rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The 2-state model shows a strong reduction in AIC compared to a 1-state model.
source: Figure 3D shows the AIC for models with discrete numbers of initiation rate states. The 2-state model shows a strong reduction in AIC compared to a 1-state model, with the 3-state model better still.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The fit to the data is continually and significantly improved by adding further initiation states beyond 3 states.
source: The curve does not plateau after the 3 state model, instead, the fit to the data is continually and significantly improved by adding further initiation states.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The most realistic interpretation is that the gene switches in activity over a spectrum or continuum of states, rather than a small number of discrete activity states.
source: The most realistic interpretation of the continually improving fit with more states is that the gene switches in activity over a spectrum or continuum of states, rather than a small number of discrete activity states.
evidence: This is an inference from the HMM analysis.

claim: The optimal 3-state fit reveals strongly non-Poisson distributions for the predicted number of polymerases initiated per frame in each state.
source: Figure 3E shows strongly non-Poisson distributions for the predicted number of polymerases initiated per frame in each state of the three state model, inconsistent with a constant initiation rate within each state.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The wide polymerase distributions imply either that the initiation rate is varying within a state, or that transitions are occurring between states on a timescale significantly faster than the frame interval.
source: The wide polymerase distributions imply either that the initiation rate is varying within a state, or that transitions are occurring between states on a timescale significantly faster than the frame interval.
evidence: This is an inference from the polymerase distributions.

claim: The cumulative polymerase plot is composed of linear segments representing periods of time over which the initiation rate is constant.
source: For a typical cell in the experimental data, the cumulative polymerase plot is composed of linear segments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) representing periods of time over which the initiation rate is constant.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A diversity of gradients in the cumulative polymerase plot indicates a spectrum of initiation rates.
source: We measured the initiation rate using an edge-preserving smoothing filter and found a diversity of such gradients, indicating a spectrum of initiation rates, again implying the transcriptional behaviour is not adequately described by a few discrete levels of activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis.

claim: The timescale of initiation rate variation through the spectrum of activity states is around 5–6 min.
source: The timescale of initiation rate variation through this spectrum of activity states can be determined using an autocorrelation analysis of non-zero initiation rates. Figure 3F shows such a plot, which reveals the initiation rate fluctuates with an average timescale of around 5–6 min, although it is possible for a roughly constant initiation rate to be sustained for up to 15 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: It is possible for a roughly constant initiation rate to be sustained for up to 15 min.
source: Figure 3F shows such a plot, which reveals the initiation rate fluctuates with an average timescale of around 5–6 min, although it is possible for a roughly constant initiation rate to be sustained for up to 15 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elongation rates fluctuating independently for each polymerase cannot produce any differences in the FRAP recovery curves.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, elongation rates fluctuating independently for each polymerase cannot produce any differences in the recovery curves.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Independent fluctuations in polymerase elongation cannot account for the fluctuations in spot intensity in the continuum model.
source: Thus independent fluctuations in polymerase elongation cannot account for the fluctuations in spot intensity in the continuum model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulations.

claim: Global fluctuations in the elongation rate give rise to different recovery curves for different spot intensities.
source: In contrast, global fluctuations in the elongation rate give rise to different recovery curves for different spot intensities (Figure 4B), as the brightest spots tend to be caused by slow-moving polymerases staying at the transcription site for longer, while the intermediate spots have a bias towards faster moving polymerases.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gene-wide fluctuations in the elongation rate may be present on a timescale of up to around 40 s without being apparent in experimental FRAP recovery curves.
source: The point at which the simulated data becomes consistent with the experimental traces (Figure 2D) is around the lower two panels of Figure 4B, that is, an elongation fluctuation timescale with an upper limit of around 10-40 s. What this effectively means is that gene-wide fluctuations in the elongation rate may be present on a timescale of up to around 40 s without being apparent in experimental FRAP recovery curves.
evidence: This is derived from comparison of simulations with experimental data.

claim: Some degree of elongation fluctuation may contribute to the temporal variation of the transcription spot intensity.
source: The exact timescale depends also on the magnitude of the fluctuations, taken here to be around 50% of the mean elongation rate, nevertheless, some degree of elongation fluctuation may contribute to the temporal variation of the transcription spot intensity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulations.

claim: For the 43 s timescale, the magnitude of the improvement in AIC is comparable to that observed experimentally.
source: For the 43 s timescale, the magnitude of the improvement is comparable to that observed experimentally.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The 43 s timescale elongation fluctuations can potentially recapitulate the variability in spot intensities observed in experiments.
source: This suggests these elongation fluctuations can potentially recapitulate the variability in spot intensities observed in experiments, with two important caveats.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulations.

claim: The super-Poissonian behaviour of the experimental data is not reproduced by training the three state model on in silico elongation fluctuation data.
source: This super-Poissonian behaviour of the experimental data is not reproduced by training the same three state model on in silico elongation fluctuation data (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating further complexity in the experimental data not fully explained by the simple elongation fluctuations.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both TATA mutant lines displayed a slight reduction in overall spot intensity.
source: Both TATA mutant lines displayed a slight reduction in overall spot intensity (Figure 5B), with FRAP experiments suggesting a similar dwell time to wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FRAP experiments suggest TATA mutants have a similar dwell time to wild type.
source: Both TATA mutant lines displayed a slight reduction in overall spot intensity (Figure 5B), with FRAP experiments suggesting a similar dwell time to wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The TATA mutants spend less time in medium and high initiation rate states, and more time at lower initiation rates, compared to control cells.
source: Analysis of time-lapse experiments using the polymerase HMM framework found that the TATA mutants spend less time in medium and high initiation rate states, and more time at lower initiation rates, compared to control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The overall timescale of initiation rate variability was not substantially changed by TATA mutations.
source: The overall timescale of initiation rate variability, measured through autocorrelation, was not substantially changed (Figure 5D) with both the wild-type and TATA mutations showing fluctuation timescales of several minutes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No clear difference in switching rates between the inactive and active states was observed for TATA mutants.
source: In addition, we observed no clear difference in switching rates between the inactive and active states.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The rate of switching to the inactive state, k(off), was unchanged between wild-type and TATA mutants.
source: The rate of switching to the inactive state, k(off), was unchanged between wild-type and TATA mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The tendency of spots to appear, k(on), showed a slight impairment in A2C mutants, although this was not statistically significant.
source: The tendency of spots to appear, k(on), showed a slight impairment in A2C mutants, although this was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: For all cell lines, both wild-type and TATA mutant, high initiation rates had a tendency to revert to lower initiation rates, and lower initiation rates had a tendency to revert to higher initiation rates.
source: For all cell lines, both wild-type and TATA mutant, high initiation rates had a tendency to revert to lower initiation rates, and lower initiation rates had a tendency to revert to higher initiation rates.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the TATA mutants, the initiation rate is less likely to switch to a higher activity state, resulting in reduced time spent in high activity states.
source: In the TATA mutants, the initiation rate is less likely to switch to a higher activity state, resulting in reduced time spent in high activity states.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: Perturbing the TATA box does not affect the duration or frequency of active states, but rather modulates the initiation rates that are possible.
source: Together these observations suggest that perturbing the TATA box does not affect the duration or frequency of active states, but rather modulates the initiation rates that are possible.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the TATA mutant analysis.

claim: The continuum model may be consistent with a recent theoretical model which proposed rapid switching between states as an improvement over the standard 2-state model in terms of information transmission.
source: Our continuum model may be consistent with a recent theoretical model (Rieckh and Tkačik, 2014) which proposed rapid switching between states as an improvement over the standard 2-state model in terms of information transmission (Figure 6—figure supplement 1iii).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior theoretical work.

claim: The initiation rate fluctuations can be thought of as the fraction of time for which the factors required for initiation are bound to the promoter.
source: In this view the initiation rate fluctuations can be thought of as the fraction of time for which the factors required for initiation are bound to the promoter.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the continuum model.

claim: When the TATA box is mutated, the overall decreased initiation rate in the active state may reflect the reduced rate of binding of necessary transcription factors.
source: When the TATA box is mutated, the overall decreased initiation rate in the active state may reflect the reduced rate of binding of necessary transcription factors, and therefore reduced occupancy of the initiating state (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TATA mutant data.

claim: The optimal discrete 3-state model consigns polymerase initiations to non-Poissonian states, which implies either multiple initiation rates within a state or switching between the discrete states faster than the imaging frame interval.
source: Illustrating the potential equivalence of this rapid switching model with our continuum model, our data show that the optimal discrete 3-state model consigns polymerase initiations to non-Poissonian states (Figure 3E), which implies either multiple initiation rates within a state (in other words more than 3 states) or switching between the discrete states faster than the imaging frame interval.
evidence: This is an inference from the HMM analysis.

claim: The distribution of cytoplasmic mRNA molecules from the continuum model was well fit to a standard two-state bursting model using a negative binomial function.
source: The distribution of cytoplasmic mRNA molecules was well fit to a standard two-state bursting model (Singer et al., 2014), using a negative binomial function (see appendix) capturing primarily the long timescale activity intervals (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When measured in the steady state using methods such as RNA FISH, a continuum of transcriptional states will appear to consist of far fewer states than can be detected using live cell approaches.
source: In other words, when measured in the steady state, using methods such as RNA FISH, a continuum of transcriptional states will appear to consist of far fewer states than can be detected using live cell approaches, highlighting the different timescales measured by different methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulations comparing live and fixed measurements.

claim: The two-state model approximates the magnitude and broad timescale of transcriptional variability.
source: The two-state model approximates the magnitude and broad timescale of transcriptional variability, although it should be noted that the bursting parameters extracted may not directly correspond to the physical quantities of burst size and frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the two-state model.

claim: The behaviour is not consistent with either constitutive, Poissonian activity or switching between a small number of discrete activity states.
source: We interpreted fluctuations in the intensity of the transcription site in terms of the time-resolved rate of polymerase initiation, and found that the behaviour is not consistent with either constitutive, Poissonian activity or switching between a small number of discrete activity states.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: A spectrum of activity states is characterised by an initiation rate varying over timescales of several minutes.
source: Instead, we observed a spectrum of activity states, characterised by an initiation rate varying over timescales of several minutes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: This spectrum of activity may be produced by very short periods of transcription initiation, where the activity lifetime or rate of reactivation is dependent on the time-varying local activity of molecular factors.
source: This spectrum of activity may be produced by very short periods of transcription initiation, where the activity lifetime or rate of reactivation is dependent on the time-varying local activity of molecular factors, or the gene locus switching between different topological conformations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: When integrated over the retention time of nascent RNA at the transcription site, 'microbursting' behaviour would give rise to a continuum of initiation rates.
source: When integrated over the retention time of nascent RNA at the transcription site, this 'microbursting' behaviour would give rise to a continuum of initiation rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the continuum arises.

claim: For act5, timescales of variation of minutes were observed by autocorrelation or Gibbs sampling of initiation rates.
source: This model is equivalent to a limiting case of our continuum model with infinitesimally slow variation in the activation rate, however, for act5 we observed timescales of variation of minutes by autocorrelation or Gibbs sampling of initiation rates.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Live cell analysis of nascent RNA dynamics allows the timescales of fluctuation to be directly extracted from the data, which is not possible from measurements of protein abundance or steady state transcript counts.
source: Alternatively, the differences may arise because live cell analysis of nascent RNA dynamics allows the timescales of fluctuation to be directly extracted from the data, which is not possible from measurements of protein abundance or steady state transcript counts.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodologies.

claim: A simple system with constant promoter activity predicts exponential distributions of transcriptional pulses and intervals.
source: To investigate the molecular origins of the bursting phenomenon, we constructed a simple theory of Poissonian transcription of the MS2 system. Unexpectedly, this simple system with constant promoter activity predicts exponential distributions of transcriptional pulses and intervals, with the pulse duration determined not only by the promoter initiation rate but also by the frame interval of observations and threshold of spot detection.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: An upper limit for the timescales of elongation rate fluctuations is around 40 s.
source: This is illustrated by our analysis of the fluctuations in the elongation rate, where, in comparison with experimental data, we estimated an upper limit for the timescales of fluctuations at around 40 s.
evidence: This is derived from FRAP simulations.

claim: Elongation rate fluctuations could not account entirely for the complexity of the spectrum of transcriptional states, although they could potentially contribute.
source: Analysis of elongation rate changes suggested such fluctuations could not account entirely for the complexity of the spectrum of transcriptional states, although they could potentially contribute.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: A low level of basal transcription cannot be ruled out in the inactive state due to the current detection threshold.
source: Due to the current detection threshold of our system, a low level of basal transcription cannot be ruled out in this inactive state.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental system.

claim: The longer periods of inactivity may reflect slower dynamics of the remodelling of chromatin, rather than binding of specific transcriptional regulators.
source: Consistent with early views of bursting (Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008), the longer periods of inactivity may reflect slower dynamics of the remodelling of chromatin, rather than binding of specific transcriptional regulators, based upon our perturbation of the core promoter.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TATA mutant data.

claim: Neither TATA box mutation studied abrogated transcription entirely.
source: Importantly, neither TATA box mutation we studied abrogated transcription entirely, as might be expected if the pre-initiation complex can no longer bind the promoter.
evidence: This is an observation from the TATA mutant experiments.

claim: A reduction in the duration of periods of high activity might suggest an impaired duration or frequency of binding, or disruption of normal promoter conformational switches in response to binding.
source: A reduction in the duration of periods of high activity might suggest an impaired duration or frequency of binding, or disruption of normal promoter conformational switches in response to binding (Gietl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TATA mutant data.

claim: The strong effects of TATA mutations in yeast and plasmid systems may reflect more simple promoter architectures.
source: The strong effects of TATA mutations in yeast and plasmid systems (Patwardhan et al., 2009; Raser and O'Shea, 2004) may reflect more simple promoter architectures.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work.

claim: In more complex systems, the potential for many inputs to transcriptional regulation will buffer the disruption of any single input.
source: In more complex systems, the potential for many inputs to transcriptional regulation will buffer the disruption of any single input (Perry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Most of the Dictyostelium actin gene family, including act5, show some developmental regulation, at least at the transcript level.
source: The gene is strongly expressed and actin is usually put under the umbrella of 'housekeeping', which is a slight simplification as most of the Dictyostelium actin gene family, including act5, show some developmental regulation, at least at the transcript level (Muramoto et al., 2012; Joseph et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Even in cases with more prominent bursting, the initiation rate in the active state is likely to fluctuate over time and differ from cell to cell.
source: However, even in cases with more prominent bursting we would argue that the initiation rate in the active state is likely to fluctuate over time and differ from cell to cell.
evidence: This is a generalization of the findings.

claim: Recent studies on mammalian transcriptional induction suggest more complexity than a standard 2-state model provides.
source: This is supported by recent studies on mammalian transcriptional induction by serum and growth factors, which also suggest more complexity than a standard 2-state model provides, with evidence from luciferase reporter fluctuations (Molina et al., 2013) and measurements of nascent RNA by smFISH indicating modulation of the transcription rate within the ON state (Senecal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A recent smFISH study revealed modulation of burst size and frequency by cell size and cycle stage, respectively.
source: A more recent smFISH study quantifying nascent RNA revealed modulation of burst size and frequency by cell size and cycle stage, respectively (Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The act5 promoter is less than 700 bp long.
source: Whilst we have argued here for a more complex view of transcriptional regulation, it must be considered that the act5 promoter is less than 700 bp long, the gene contains no introns and around 60% of the Dictyostelium genome encodes protein (Eichinger et al., 2005), and so provides little scope for long range regulatory interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the gene studied.

evidence: This is a description of the gene studied.

claim: Around 60% of the Dictyostelium genome encodes protein.

claim: There are perhaps a hundred different proteins involved in a standard eukaryotic transcription reaction.
source: There are perhaps a hundred different proteins involved in a standard eukaryotic transcription reaction, even ignoring the components of the chromatin template.
evidence: This is general knowledge about transcription.

claim: The likely configurational complexity, in addition to the potential for modulation by protein modification and nuclear context, seems consistent with the continuum view.
